unit_name: Strategies using Exchange Traded Currency Derivatives
overview: This chapter is where the real action happens. In Unit 3 and 4, you learned what Futures and Options are. In Unit 5, you will learn HOW to actually use them in real life. We will look at three main types of players: Hedgers (who want safety), Speculators (who want profit), and Arbitrageurs (who want risk-free money). The exam will test this chapter using practical 'scenario-based' questions. They will give you a story about an importer or an exporter and ask you to choose the correct strategy to save them from a loss.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Hedging means taking a position in the futures market that is exactly OPPOSITE to your risk in the real world. This locks in your price and protects your business from currency fluctuations.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Let us break this down into two simple steps based on who you are:

Scenario A: The Importer (Long Hedge)
Step 1: An importer buys goods from the US and has to PAY Dollars in the future. 
Step 2: Their biggest fear: 'What if the Dollar becomes very expensive (Rupee weakens)?'
Step 3: Strategy: To lock in the buying price, the importer will BUY USDINR Futures today. This is called a 'Long Hedge'. If the Dollar goes up, they pay more in the real world, but they make a matching profit in the futures market.

Scenario B: The Exporter (Short Hedge)
Step 1: An exporter sells software to the US and will RECEIVE Dollars in the future.
Step 2: Their biggest fear: 'What if the Dollar value crashes (Rupee strengthens)? I will get fewer Rupees!'
Step 3: Strategy: To lock in the selling price, the exporter will SELL USDINR Futures today. This is called a 'Short Hedge'.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: This is guaranteed to be in the exam. You will be given a 3-line case study and asked 'What should the exporter do?'. You must know exactly whether to Buy or Sell.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
An Indian electronics shop is importing iPhones worth $10,000. Payment is due in 1 month. Current spot is ₹83.00. 1-month future is ₹83.20.
Fear: Dollar might go to ₹85.
Action: Shop owner BUYS 10 lots (10 x $1000) of 1-month USDINR Futures at ₹83.20.
Result: No matter what happens in the spot market next month, his effective cost is locked at exactly ₹83.20 per dollar.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: Reliance Industries imports crude oil and pays in billions of Dollars. To avoid surprises in their raw material cost, they heavily BUY USDINR Futures (Long Hedge). Infosys exports IT services and receives Dollars. To secure their Rupee profits, they SELL USDINR Futures (Short Hedge).
exam_traps: Mixing up Importer and Exporter actions. REMEMBER: Importer = Needs to Buy USD = BUYS Futures. Exporter = Needs to Sell USD = SELLS Futures.
Thinking hedging gives extra profit. False. Hedging only PREVENTS loss by fixing the price. You give up the chance of extra profit for the guarantee of safety.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Importer = INcoming goods, OUTgoing Dollars. Fears Dollar going UP. So, BUY Futures (Long). Exporter = OUTgoing goods, INcoming Dollars. Fears Dollar going DOWN. So, SELL Futures (Short).

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Hedging with Futures is strict—you are locked in. Hedging with Options is like buying insurance. You are protected from the bad stuff, but you can still enjoy the good stuff if the market moves in your favor.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Let's look at how Importers and Exporters use Options:

Scenario A: The Importer (Buys a Call Option)
Step 1: The importer has to pay Dollars. They fear the Dollar will rise.
Step 2: They BUY a USDINR Call Option (Right to buy Dollars at a fixed Strike Price) and pay a premium.
Step 3: If Dollar shoots up to ₹86, they use the Call Option and buy cheaply at their Strike Price (say, ₹83).
Step 4: If Dollar crashes to ₹80, they simply throw the option away (losing only the premium) and buy Dollars super cheap from the open market at ₹80!

Scenario B: The Exporter (Buys a Put Option)
Step 1: The exporter will receive Dollars. They fear the Dollar will fall.
Step 2: They BUY a USDINR Put Option (Right to sell Dollars at a fixed Strike Price).
Step 3: If Dollar falls to ₹80, they use the Put Option and sell at their high Strike Price (say, ₹83).
Step 4: If Dollar shoots up to ₹86, they throw the option away and happily sell their dollars in the open market for ₹86.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: The exam tests if you understand the advantage of Options over Futures. Options allow you to walk away if the spot market offers a better deal.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Effective Cost for Importer = Spot Price Paid (or Strike Price if exercised) + Premium Paid
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: When an importer uses an option, their final cost is whatever they paid for the dollars, PLUS the non-refundable premium they paid for the option ticket.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
Exporter expects $1,000. He Buys a Put Option at Strike ₹83 by paying a Premium of ₹0.50.
Case 1: Market falls to ₹80. He exercises the Put. Sells at ₹83. His net realization = 83 - 0.50 (premium) = ₹82.50.
Case 2: Market rises to ₹85. He ignores the Put. Sells in the open market at ₹85. His net realization = 85 - 0.50 (premium) = ₹84.50.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: A diamond merchant in Surat is expecting payment from Belgium in Euros. He isn't sure if the Euro will go up or down, but he cannot afford it to go below ₹90. He buys a EURINR Put Option at a ₹90 strike. It acts purely as a safety net (insurance floor).
exam_traps: Thinking the hedger SELLS options. Usually, hedgers BUY options (pay premium) to get the safe 'Right to choose'. Speculators are the ones who usually sell options.
Forgetting to deduct/add the premium when calculating the final effective price.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Importer wants to BUY Dollars = Buys CALL Option. Exporter wants to SELL Dollars = Buys PUT Option.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Speculators do not have any real business involving dollars. They are purely trading to make a profit by guessing the direction of the market.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Step 1: Bullish View (Market will go UP). A speculator thinks RBI will cut interest rates and USDINR will rise. They will either BUY Futures or BUY Call Options. Both strategies make money when the price goes up.
Step 2: Bearish View (Market will go DOWN). A speculator thinks the Indian economy is booming and the Rupee will get very strong (USDINR will fall). They will either SELL Futures or BUY Put Options. Both strategies make money when the price goes down.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: You need to map the market view (Bullish/Bearish) to the correct instrument.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: A college student sitting in Delhi watches the US election results. He thinks the Dollar will crash. He opens his broker app and Buys 5 lots of USDINR Put Options. He is a pure speculator taking a calculated risk.
exam_traps: Confusing Hedging and Speculation. Hedging = Reducing Risk. Speculation = Taking on Risk for profit.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Bullish (Up) = Buy Future / Buy Call. Bearish (Down) = Sell Future / Buy Put.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Arbitrage means finding a mispricing between two markets and making a 100% risk-free profit by buying cheap in one and selling expensive in the other at the exact same time.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Step 1: In a perfect world, Future Price = Spot Price + Interest Cost.
Step 2: Sometimes, because of panic or high demand, the Future Price shoots up way too high. It becomes overpriced.
Step 3: An Arbitrageur spots this. They instantly SELL the overpriced Future contract.
Step 4: At the exact same second, they borrow Rupees, BUY the actual Dollars in the Spot market (which is cheap), and hold them in a bank to earn interest.
Step 5: On the expiry day, they deliver the Dollars they hold to settle the Future contract. The profit is guaranteed from day one. This is called 'Cash and Carry Arbitrage'.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Arbitrageurs are important because they force prices back to normal. The exam will ask you what an arbitrageur does if futures are overpriced.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: A huge bank's computer algorithm notices that USDINR Spot is ₹83.00, but on the NSE, a 1-month future is trading at ₹84.00 (which is absurdly high). The computer instantly sells the ₹84 Future and buys the ₹83 Spot. It locks in a massive risk-free profit of ₹1 per dollar in milliseconds.
exam_traps: Thinking Arbitrage has risk. Arbitrage strictly means ZERO risk.
If Future is overpriced -> Sell Future, Buy Spot. If Future is underpriced -> Buy Future, Sell Spot.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Arbitrage = Always Right. You buy the cheaper one and sell the expensive one simultaneously.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Sometimes you know the market is going to explode, but you don't know in WHICH direction. Straddles and Strangles are option combinations used to make money from huge price jumps in ANY direction.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Step 1: Long Straddle: You Buy a Call Option AND Buy a Put Option of the EXACT SAME Strike Price and same expiry. 
Why? If the market shoots UP, your Call makes huge money (Put becomes zero). If the market crashes DOWN, your Put makes huge money (Call becomes zero). As long as it moves big, you win. The only way you lose is if the market stays completely flat (because you paid two premiums).
Step 2: Long Strangle: You Buy an Out-Of-The-Money (OTM) Call AND an OTM Put. 
Why? It is exactly like a Straddle, but because you are buying OTM options, the premiums are much cheaper. The catch? The market needs to move even FASTER and BIGGER for you to make a profit.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Very popular exam question. You must know the difference between a Straddle (same strike) and Strangle (different strikes).
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Maximum Loss for Long Straddle/Strangle = Total Premium Paid (Call Premium + Put Premium)
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: Because you are buying two options, you are paying two non-refundable ticket fees. If the market doesn't move at all, both options expire useless, and you lose both premiums.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
Spot is ₹83.
Straddle: Buy 83 Call (Premium ₹0.50) + Buy 83 Put (Premium ₹0.50). Total cost = ₹1.00. You need the market to go above ₹84 or below ₹82 to make a profit.
Strangle: Buy 84 Call (Premium ₹0.20) + Buy 82 Put (Premium ₹0.20). Total cost = ₹0.40. Cheaper! But you need the market to go above ₹84.40 or below ₹81.60 to make a profit.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: Tomorrow is the Union Budget announcement by the Finance Minister, or the RBI Governor's policy speech. A trader knows the Rupee will swing wildly but doesn't know if it will be good or bad news. He buys a Long Straddle today.
exam_traps: Confusing Straddle with Strangle. Straddle = SAME Strike (e.g., Buy 83 Call + Buy 83 Put). Strangle = DIFFERENT Strikes (e.g., Buy 84 Call + Buy 82 Put).
Thinking these strategies make money in a quiet market. They strictly need high volatility (big moves) to work.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Straddle = Riding a horse (legs on the SAME saddle/strike). Strangle = Choking from two DIFFERENT sides (different strikes).

important_differences.difference_between: Hedging with Futures vs Hedging with Options
important_differences.clear_explanation: Futures lock you into a fixed price; you are protected from losses but you also give up any chance of extra profit if the market moves favorably. Options act like insurance; you pay an upfront premium and are protected from losses, but if the market moves favorably, you can simply ignore the option and take the extra profit in the spot market.

Both are used when you expect a big price movement but don't know the direction. A Straddle involves buying a Call and a Put at the EXACT SAME strike price (higher cost, closer breakeven). A Strangle involves buying a Call and a Put at DIFFERENT, Out-Of-The-Money strike prices (lower cost, but needs a much larger price movement to make a profit).

frequently_asked_exam_areas: Identifying the correct Hedge: Importer buys futures/calls. Exporter sells futures/buys puts.
Calculating the final effective price for an importer/exporter using options (remember to factor in the premium!).
Identifying a Straddle (Same strike Call + Put) vs a Strangle (Different strike Call + Put).
Understanding the motive of an Arbitrageur (Risk-free profit from mispricing).
quick_revision_summary: Hedgers want safety. Speculators want profit. Arbitrageurs want risk-free gaps.
Importer = Has to pay Dollars = Fears Dollar rising = Buys USD Future or Buys Call Option.
Exporter = Has to receive Dollars = Fears Dollar falling = Sells USD Future or Buys Put Option.
Arbitrage is perfectly risk-free and usually involves zero net investment.
Long Straddle = Buy Call + Buy Put at the SAME strike price.
Long Strangle = Buy Call + Buy Put at DIFFERENT strike prices (usually OTM).
Volatility strategies (Straddle/Strangle) lose money if the market remains flat.
